content_html:
Designed vs. Evolutionary

Evolution produces systems that are highly optimized for survival and energetic efficiency under historical constraints, but they are not tidy or globally optimized like engineered designs. They exhibit redundancy, path dependence, and “tinkered” solutions that are robust and adaptable.

Why “optimized yet messy”?

  • Energy efficiency: Neural signaling is costly; brains economize spikes and wiring. The adult human brain performs impressively on ~20 W, prioritizing metabolic efficiency over neat design.
  • Robustness & degeneracy: Multiple different components can produce similar functions; redundancy supports fault tolerance.
  • Historical constraints: Evolution “tinkers” with available parts; structures are repurposed rather than rebuilt from scratch.

References

  1. Evolution as “tinkering,” not top-down design — Jacob (1977), Science: Evolution and tinkering.
  2. Spandrels & constraints in evolution — Gould & Lewontin (1979): The spandrels of San Marco.
  3. Energy budgets of neural signaling — Attwell & Laughlin (2001): An energy budget for signaling; Lennie (2003): Cost of cortical computation.
  4. Metabolic limits & brain efficiency — Niven & Laughlin (2008): Energy limitation as a selective pressure; Herculano-Houzel (2011): Scaling of brain metabolism with neurons.
  5. Robustness & degeneracy in biological systems — Kitano (2004): Biological robustness; Edelman & Gally (2001): Degeneracy and complexity.
